title: How High Expectations Can Improve Performance
paragraphs: For more than half a century, researchers have found that when teachers expect a lot from their students, those students tend to do better. This is known as the Pygmalion effect, named after a sculptor in Greek mythology whose statue came to life. However, a new study suggests that simply having high expectations is not enough. How those expectations are communicated also matters.

The study, which will be published in the journal Educational Researcher, was led by Yasemin Copur-Gencturk, a professor of teacher education at the University of Southern California. Nearly 1,000 math teachers took part. They watched recordings of middle school students explaining their answers to math problems, some of which were wrong or only partly correct. Some teachers were asked to give feedback as usual, while others were asked to focus on high standards and expectations.

The teachers who were asked to focus on high expectations gave more specific feedback. They were 13 percentage points more likely to discuss students' strengths and weaknesses. However, only about one in ten teachers in both groups gave students specific advice on how to correct their mistakes.

The researchers also found some worrying patterns. Teachers who were asked to convey high expectations often did so by saying that a student was not trying hard enough. According to the researchers, this kind of feedback is less effective when it does not include specific examples and strategies. In addition, girls were more likely to receive negative comments about their math ability and effort.

Copur-Gencturk explained that asking teachers to hold high standards makes them more specific, but they still do not give detailed feedback on students' strategies and performance. She added that teachers have few chances to practice this kind of feedback, and that it is not an easy skill to learn.

Other researchers have described a better approach. David Yeager of the University of Texas at Austin uses the term "wise feedback" to describe comments that combine high expectations with support to help students meet them. According to research, students perform better when they receive this kind of feedback.
